clue.text: Dash off to escape withstimulating author

parts.note: to dash off a note is to pen it, writing quickly
to elope is to run away secretly, an escape
lively means stimulating or spirited

explanation.surface: A reader rushes away from a book by an author they find exciting.
explanation.walkthrough: PENELOPE LIVELY is the English novelist who won the Booker Prize for Moon Tiger; 'with' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Penelope Lively is a prize-winning English novelist and children's writer.

clue.text: Anti-Establishment treatment of Pushkin

indicators.note: a treatment of a text reworks it, so the poet's name is rearranged

explanation.surface: A radical director's version of a Russian poet's work.
explanation.definitionFit: Punk culture defied the establishment, so something in its spirit is rebellious.

clue.text: Young dogs biting foot of papergirl delivering specialistpublications

parts.note: young means new

indicators.note: the puppies biting something hold it in their mouths, so a letter goes inside

parts.note: setters are a breed of gun dog

indicators.note: the foot of a word in a down clue is its final letter

explanation.surface: Puppies nip at a paper girl's ankle as she does her round with trade journals.
explanation.walkthrough: The paper-round surface hides that 'biting' is a container signal: the puppies hold the paper girl's last letter in their jaws, just after the fourth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Bulletins sent to members or subscribers on one subject are specialist periodicals.

clue.text: Counterculture figure who produced nonsense on ecstasy ultimately

parts.note: Edward Lear wrote nonsense verse such as The Owl and the Pussy-Cat

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word it follows

explanation.surface: A sixties guru talked gibberish while high on drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: Timothy LEARY was the 1960s psychologist who promoted LSD; 'on' only joins the pieces, and ecstasy fits his scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Timothy Leary was an icon of the 1960s hippie movement, urging people to 'turn on, tune in, drop out'.

clue.text: Ex-prisoner, oldone who wrote about lawyer being below acceptable standard

parts.note: par is the normal or expected standard, as in 'up to par'
Harper Lee wrote To Kill a Mockingbird, whose hero is the lawyer Atticus Finch

explanation.surface: A released convict and an elderly writer discuss a substandard attorney.
explanation.walkthrough: 'below acceptable standard' looks like one phrase meaning poor; 'being below' says the other pieces come under PAR in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone let out of jail early on conditions of good behaviour is a released inmate under supervision.

clue.text: Private Angelo producer: I'm tapped to bring page to screen subsequently

parts.words: I'm tapped to bring page to screen
parts.note: a hyperlink is tapped on a phone to bring up a web page
later means subsequently

explanation.surface: A film studio talks of adapting a novel for cinema at some later date.
explanation.walkthrough: Eric LINKLATER, the Scottish novelist, wrote Private Angelo (1946); 'bring page to screen' reads like adapting a book for film.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric Linklater wrote the comic war novel Private Angelo, so he produced it.

clue.text: Vera, at length, just introduced a Scottish crime writer to her friends

definitions.text: a Scottish crime writer to her friends

indicators.note: only the opening of each word is introduced, so take the first letters

explanation.surface: Vera talks at length, having just met a Scottish novelist among her friends.
explanation.walkthrough: Val McDermid is the Scottish crime novelist; friends would call her by the short form of Valerie. Vera also hints at Ann Cleeves's detective.
explanation.definitionFit: Val McDermid, the Scottish crime novelist, goes by the familiar short form of her first name.

clue.text: Scrolling regularly has turned up nothing on subject of George Saunders

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed above the next piece
in a down clue, turned up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: nil means nothing

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of the word, here the even ones

explanation.surface: Someone scrolling on a phone keeps finding nothing about an American author's subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned up' reverses NIL to LIN; the even letters of 'Scrolling' give COLN. Saunders's Booker winner is Lincoln in the Bardo.
explanation.definitionFit: George Saunders's novel Lincoln in the Bardo centres on Abraham Lincoln mourning his son.

clue.text: He considered the arts/science divide small these days

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
now means at present, these days

explanation.surface: A thinker judged the gap between arts and sciences to be shrinking nowadays.
explanation.walkthrough: C. P. SNOW's 1959 lecture The Two Cultures argued that the arts and sciences had split apart.
explanation.definitionFit: C. P. Snow's lecture The Two Cultures analysed the gulf between scientists and literary intellectuals.

clue.text: Effect of thriller read out by figure captivating nearly everyone

indicators.note: out describes the letters of the word read as put out of order
captivating means holding prisoner, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: nine is a figure, a number

indicators.note: nearly means not quite complete, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: all means everyone

explanation.surface: A gripping novel is read aloud by a character who enthrals almost every listener.
explanation.walkthrough: 'read out' sounds like a homophone signal, but 'out' marks an anagram; 'nearly' trims the word for everyone and 'captivating' sets the result in the number.
explanation.definitionFit: A thriller sets the reader's pulse racing, which is the hormone released by excitement or fear.

clue.text: Unwilling to commit, I'd returned Sally Rooney's second novel

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: taken as written, the letters I and D

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are put into a new order
second points to the second letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A reader admits she sent back the second book by the Irish novelist Sally Rooney.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns I'D into DI; 'novel' rearranges SALLY plus O, the second letter of 'Rooney's', into SLOYAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A disloyal person will not stay faithful, so is reluctant to commit to a cause or partner.

clue.text: Head of library would somehow find A Shropshire Lad here?

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
somehow says the letters are arranged in some other way

explanation.surface: A chief librarian wonders where to track down a copy of Housman's poems.
explanation.walkthrough: A. E. Housman's A Shropshire Lad names the Shropshire market town LUDLOW, where his ashes lie.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shropshire market town features in Housman's poems and holds his ashes, so the lad is found there.

clue.text: "You see, but you do not observe. The is clear." (Holmes to Watson, A Scandal in Bohemia)

definitions.text: "You see, but you do not observe. The is clear." (Holmes to Watson, A Scandal in Bohemia)

parts.words: "You see, but you do not observe. The is clear." (Holmes to Watson, A Scandal in Bohemia)
parts.note: a quotation with a missing word: Holmes contrasts merely seeing with observing and says the difference between them is plain

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in the Conan Doyle quotation: the word means a difference or contrast.
explanation.definitionFit: Holmes is pointing to the clear difference between looking and noticing.

clue.text: Time sheet altered to disguise short-term worker's romance at sea

indicators.note: to disguise something is to cover it, so one piece wraps round the other
altered means changed, so the letters of sheet are rearranged

parts.note: a temp is a short-term office worker

explanation.surface: An office time sheet was falsified to hide a temp's love affair on a cruise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'altered' scrambles 'sheet' and 'to disguise' wraps it round the worker. Shakespeare's late plays are called romances, and this one opens with a storm at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's late play opening with a shipwreck is classed among his romances.

clue.text: Daydream over lothario, the lead in romantic spy tale

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means placed above the next piece

parts.note: to moon about is to daydream
a rake is a womaniser, a lothario

indicators.note: the lead in a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A dreamy reader imagines a seducer as the star of a love story.
explanation.walkthrough: Ian Fleming's James Bond novel MOONRAKER; the romance surface hides that only R is taken from 'romantic'.
explanation.definitionFit: Moonraker is one of Ian Fleming's James Bond thrillers.

clue.text: Air Dynasty?

definitions.meaning: an air is a tune, a melody to be sung
the ... dynasty ruled China from 960 to 1279

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'Dynasty' is an example: one Chinese ruling house among several.
explanation.definitionFit: A tune is something sung, and the Song were a Chinese imperial dynasty.

clue.text: A sequence of trocheesforms this line

indicators.note: a sequence of letters is a consecutive run taken from inside the word

explanation.surface: A run of stressed-unstressed feet makes up this line of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: The verse surface suggests poetry, but the OCHE is the line a darts player stands behind; it sits in 'trochees'.
explanation.definitionFit: In darts the oche is the mark on the floor that players must throw from behind.

clue.text: Rogue act heartlessly inserted into Blithe Spirit

indicators.note: inserted into says one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: blithe spirit, a happy mood, is cheer

indicators.note: heartlessly means with the middle removed, leaving the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A villainous scene is crudely added to Noel Coward's comedy Blithe Spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: Blithe Spirit is Noel Coward's comedy, but here it reads as a happy mood. 'heartlessly' strips the middle from 'act' before 'inserted into' places it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rogue cheats people, so is a swindler or cheat.

clue.text: Oldunkempt dons intimidate TrinityCollege alumnus

indicators.note: dons means puts on, so one piece is worn round the other

parts.note: to scare is to intimidate
wild means untidy, unkempt

explanation.surface: Scruffy elderly lecturers frighten a former student of a Dublin college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dons' looks like university teachers, but it means wears: the untidy word puts on the frightening one, which goes round it. Wilde studied at Trinity College Dublin.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde studied classics at Trinity College Dublin before Oxford.

clue.text: Around uni, struggling to hurriedly study Yorick, as seen in Act V

definitions.text: Yorick, as seen in Act V

indicators.note: around says the cramming goes round the other piece

parts.note: to cram is to study hurriedly for an exam

indicators.note: struggling means in difficulty, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A struggling student rushes to revise the graveyard scene of Hamlet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'struggling' scrambles 'uni' and 'Around' sets the revising round it. In Hamlet Act V the dead jester Yorick appears only as a skull.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hamlet's final act the dead jester Yorick appears only as a skull dug from his grave.

clue.text: "All the decent of life is to be rudely torn off" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France)

definitions.text: "All the decent of life is to be rudely torn off" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France)

parts.words: "All the decent of life is to be rudely torn off" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France)
parts.note: a quotation with a missing word: Burke laments that the fabric covering and adorning life will be stripped away

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in Burke's sentence: the missing word is the hanging fabric that dresses life decently.
explanation.definitionFit: Burke pictures custom as cloth hangings that decently cover life's bareness.

clue.text: Preview sample from Brontë (a serialisation)

indicators.note: sample from says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A trailer offers an extract from a serialised Brontë novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A short trailer or taste given to stir interest ahead of the full release.

clue.text: Satire about cultural elite's stunt at literature festival

parts.note: an antic is a playful trick or stunt
Hay-on-Wye in Wales holds a famous annual literature festival

explanation.surface: A satirical book about the highbrow set is a publicity stunt at a book festival.
explanation.walkthrough: Aldous Huxley's ANTIC HAY (1923) satirises London intellectuals; Hay is a Welsh town known for its book festival.
explanation.definitionFit: Aldous Huxley's novel mocks the post-war London intelligentsia.

clue.text: Smith's debut lackingElwyn Brooks's power

indicators.note: lacking means without, so one name is taken away

parts.note: Zadie Smith's first novel was White Teeth
E. B. White, author of Charlotte's Web, was Elwyn Brooks White

explanation.surface: A novelist's first book lacks the punch of a classic American writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the surname of E. B. White from Zadie Smith's debut novel title.
explanation.definitionFit: A law with teeth has real force, so the word means power or effectiveness.

clue.text: Kate Atkinson's four central characters getting cast iron implement

indicators.note: cast means thrown into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged
the central characters of a word are its middle letters, here four of them

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: Kate Atkinson's main characters are cast in a crime novel about an iron weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'four central characters' takes the middle of the surname; 'cast' scrambles those with the first name, and iron's chemical symbol follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A sharp serrated table knife is a piece of cutlery, a tool.

clue.text: Outward appearance of Apuleius'Lucius in the end?

definitions.text: Outward appearance of Apuleius'Lucius in the end?

indicators.note: the outward appearance of a word is its outer letters, first and last
in the end points to the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A reader asks how Apuleius's hero finally looked.
explanation.walkthrough: In Apuleius's The Golden Ass, Lucius is turned into a donkey, so that is his outward look; the whole clue is also the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Golden Ass the hero Lucius is transformed into a donkey.

clue.text: Fateful date (that is, for a Roman short of time)

indicators.note: short of means lacking, so a letter is removed

parts.note: id est is Latin for that is, written i.e.

explanation.surface: A doomed day is described in Latin by someone with little time.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ides of March was the day Julius Caesar was assassinated, after the soothsayer's warning.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar was warned to beware the Ides of March, the day he was murdered.

clue.text: Appointment on the phone does stuff helpful for an opinionatedgentleman

indicators.note: a word heard over the phone is judged by its sound, not spelling

parts.note: a tryst is an appointment, often between lovers
rams means stuffs or crams in
handy means helpful, useful

explanation.surface: A man on the phone arranges a meeting and crams in things useful for a talkative gent.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurence Sterne's novel is The Life and Opinions of TRISTRAM SHANDY, Gentleman, hence the opinionated gentleman.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterne's narrator is the gentleman whose life and opinions fill the novel.
